```{r}
# data loading

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(readr)
library(tidymodels)
library(stringr)
library(here)

tidymodels_prefer()

team_offense <- read_csv(here("data", "weekly_team_stats_offense.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  clean_names()

team_defense <- read_csv(here("data", "weekly_team_stats_defense.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  clean_names()

player_offense <- read_csv(here("data", "weekly_player_stats_offense.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  clean_names()

games_all <- read_csv(here("data", "nfl_all_seasons.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  clean_names()
```

Prediction Problem

The objective of this project is to predict whether an NFL team covers the closing point spread in a given game using pre-game team performance metrics, rolling team performance averages, and game-level context. The response variable is a binary indicator of spread coverage, making this a supervised classification problem. Predicting spread outcomes is difficult because betting markets incorporate large amounts of public and expert information, creating a strong baseline where naive strategies rarely exceed a 50% hit rate. The goal of the project is therefore to evaluate whether structured statistical models can identify signal beyond public narratives and market expectations.

Data Sources

This project integrates three complementary NFL datasets sourced from Kaggle.

The first dataset contains weekly player-level offensive statistics, including passing, rushing, and receiving production. These data remain useful for future feature engineering, but the PM2 modeling pipeline focuses primarily on team-level data.

The second dataset provides team-level offensive and defensive statistics, including yards, touchdowns, turnovers, snap counts, efficiency measures, and season-to-date rolling averages. These rolling-average variables are especially useful because they are known before the next game begins.

The third dataset contains historical NFL betting market data, including final scores, point spreads, totals, stadium information, and weather conditions. After purchasing the full dataset, the analysis now spans multiple seasons rather than just the small 2025 sample used in Progress Memo 1.

All datasets share common identifiers such as season, week, and team, allowing them to be reshaped into a unified team-game modeling dataset.

```{r}
# team lookup and normalization helpers

team_lookup <- tribble(
  ~team_name, ~team,
  "Arizona Cardinals", "ARI",
  "Atlanta Falcons", "ATL",
  "Baltimore Ravens", "BAL",
  "Buffalo Bills", "BUF",
  "Carolina Panthers", "CAR",
  "Chicago Bears", "CHI",
  "Cincinnati Bengals", "CIN",
  "Cleveland Browns", "CLE",
  "Dallas Cowboys", "DAL",
  "Denver Broncos", "DEN",
  "Detroit Lions", "DET",
  "Green Bay Packers", "GB",
  "Houston Texans", "HOU",
  "Indianapolis Colts", "IND",
  "Jacksonville Jaguars", "JAX",
  "Kansas City Chiefs", "KC",
  "Las Vegas Raiders", "LVR",
  "Oakland Raiders", "LVR",
  "Los Angeles Chargers", "LAC",
  "San Diego Chargers", "LAC",
  "Los Angeles Rams", "LAR",
  "St. Louis Rams", "LAR",
  "Miami Dolphins", "MIA",
  "Minnesota Vikings", "MIN",
  "New England Patriots", "NE",
  "New Orleans Saints", "NO",
  "New York Giants", "NYG",
  "New York Jets", "NYJ",
  "Philadelphia Eagles", "PHI",
  "Pittsburgh Steelers", "PIT",
  "San Francisco 49ers", "SF",
  "Seattle Seahawks", "SEA",
  "Tampa Bay Buccaneers", "TB",
  "Tennessee Titans", "TEN",
  "Washington Redskins", "WAS",
  "Washington Football Team", "WAS",
  "Washington Commanders", "WAS"
)

normalize_game_id <- function(x) {
  x |>
    str_replace_all("_SD_", "_LAC_") |>
    str_replace_all("_OAK_", "_LVR_") |>
    str_replace_all("_STL_", "_LAR_") |>
    str_replace_all("_LA_", "_LAR_")
}

normalize_team <- function(x) {
  case_when(
    x == "LV" ~ "LVR",
    x == "LA" ~ "LAR",
    TRUE ~ x
  )
}
```

```{r}
# betting data to regular-season team-game rows

games_reg <- games_all |>
  filter(schedule_season >= 2012, schedule_playoff == FALSE) |>
  mutate(schedule_week = as.integer(schedule_week)) |>
  left_join(team_lookup, by = c("team_home" = "team_name")) |>
  rename(home_team = team) |>
  left_join(team_lookup, by = c("team_away" = "team_name")) |>
  rename(away_team = team) |>
  mutate(
    team_favorite_id = normalize_team(team_favorite_id)
  )

games_team <- games_reg |>
  mutate(
    season = schedule_season,
    week = schedule_week,
    season_type = "REG",
    game_id_norm = str_c(
      schedule_season,
      "_",
      str_pad(schedule_week, width = 2, side = "left", pad = "0"),
      "_",
      away_team,
      "_",
      home_team
    )
  ) |>
  transmute(
    game_id_norm,
    season,
    week,
    season_type,
    team_norm = home_team,
    opponent = away_team,
    home_away = "home",
    team_favorite_id,
    team_score = score_home,
    opponent_score = score_away,
    spread_favorite,
    over_under_line,
    stadium,
    stadium_neutral,
    weather_temperature,
    weather_wind_mph,
    weather_humidity
  ) |>
  bind_rows(
    games_reg |>
      mutate(
        season = schedule_season,
        week = schedule_week,
        season_type = "REG",
        game_id_norm = str_c(
          schedule_season,
          "_",
          str_pad(schedule_week, width = 2, side = "left", pad = "0"),
          "_",
          away_team,
          "_",
          home_team
        )
      ) |>
      transmute(
        game_id_norm,
        season,
        week,
        season_type,
        team_norm = away_team,
        opponent = home_team,
        home_away = "away",
        team_favorite_id,
        team_score = score_away,
        opponent_score = score_home,
        spread_favorite,
        over_under_line,
        stadium,
        stadium_neutral,
        weather_temperature,
        weather_wind_mph,
        weather_humidity
      )
  )
```


```{r}
# normalize weekly team files and join

team_offense_clean <- team_offense |>
  mutate(
    game_id_norm = normalize_game_id(game_id),
    team_norm = normalize_team(team)
  )

team_defense_clean <- team_defense |>
  mutate(
    game_id_norm = normalize_game_id(game_id),
    team_norm = normalize_team(team)
  )

model_data <- games_team |>
  left_join(
    team_offense_clean,
    by = c("game_id_norm", "season", "week", "season_type", "team_norm")
  ) |>
  left_join(
    team_defense_clean,
    by = c("game_id_norm", "season", "week", "season_type", "team_norm"),
    suffix = c("_off", "_def")
  )
```

Data Preparation

The full betting file is first filtered to regular-season games from 2012 onward so that it lines up with the weekly team datasets. Each betting-market game is then reshaped into two rows, one for each team, so that the final dataset is at the team-game level. This makes it possible to join betting context, offense, and defense into one row structure suitable for supervised learning.

```{r}
# join checks

join_check <- tibble(
  object = c("games_team", "team_offense_clean", "team_defense_clean", "model_data"),
  rows = c(
    nrow(games_team),
    nrow(team_offense_clean),
    nrow(team_defense_clean),
    nrow(model_data)
  )
)

knitr::kable(join_check)
```


```{r}
# unmatched rows and missingness check

join_diagnostics <- tibble(
  unmatched_games_team_vs_offense = games_team |>
    anti_join(
      team_offense_clean,
      by = c("game_id_norm", "season", "week", "season_type", "team_norm")
    ) |>
    nrow(),
  pct_missing_total_off_yards = mean(is.na(model_data$total_off_yards)),
  pct_missing_average_total_off_yards = mean(is.na(model_data$average_total_off_yards)),
  pct_missing_average_sack = mean(is.na(model_data$average_sack))
)

knitr::kable(join_diagnostics, digits = 3)
```


```{r}
# target variable and team-level spread

model_data <- model_data |>
  mutate(
    spread_team = if_else(team_norm == team_favorite_id, spread_favorite, -spread_favorite),
    margin = team_score - opponent_score,
    margin_vs_spread = margin + spread_team,
    cover = case_when(
      margin_vs_spread > 0 ~ "cover",
      margin_vs_spread < 0 ~ "no_cover",
      TRUE ~ "push"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(cover != "push")
```

```{r}
# cleaned modeling dataset

cleaned_model_nfl <- model_data |>
  filter(
    !is.na(average_total_off_yards),
    !is.na(average_passing_yards),
    !is.na(average_rushing_yards),
    !is.na(average_sack),
    !is.na(average_qb_hit)
  ) |>
  transmute(
    cover = factor(cover),
    home_away = factor(home_away),
    stadium_neutral = factor(stadium_neutral),
    spread_team,
    over_under_line,
    weather_temperature,
    weather_wind_mph,
    weather_humidity,
    win_pct_off,
    average_total_off_yards,
    average_pass_attempts,
    average_complete_pass,
    average_passing_yards,
    average_rush_attempts,
    average_rushing_yards,
    average_first_down_pass,
    average_first_down_rush,
    average_third_down_converted,
    average_third_down_failed,
    average_fourth_down_converted,
    average_fourth_down_failed,
    average_rush_touchdown,
    average_pass_touchdown,
    average_interception_off,
    average_fumble_lost_off,

    average_qb_hit,
```

Modeling Dataset

The final PM2 modeling dataset is called cleaned_model_nfl. It contains one row per team-game observation, a binary response variable (cover vs no_cover), and a focused predictor set made entirely of pre-game context and season-to-date rolling averages. Importantly, current-game outcomes such as team score, opponent score, and same-game offensive production are excluded from the predictor set to avoid leakage.

The final predictor set includes more than 16 variables and reflects a balanced mix of betting-market information, weather context, offensive rolling averages, and defensive rolling averages. This is an appropriate dataset for fitting the null model and an initial logistic regression model in Progress Memo 2.

Analysis Plan

The primary assessment metric for this project is ROC AUC, because the task is a binary classification problem and ROC AUC evaluates how well the model ranks likely covers versus non-covers across classification thresholds. Accuracy will also be reported as a secondary metric for interpretability.

The modeling plan uses an 80/20 initial train-test split stratified by the response variable, followed by resampling on the training data using 10-fold cross-validation. For Progress Memo 2, two model types will be fit: a baseline null model and a logistic regression classifier. A basic recipe will be used to dummy encode categorical predictors, remove zero-variance predictors, and normalize numeric predictors.

Progress Summary

Since Progress Memo 1, the project has advanced from data identification and target definition to a functional modeling dataset. The major progress in PM2 has been the acquisition of the full historical betting dataset, the construction of a team-game table, the successful join with weekly team offense and defense data, and the creation of a leakage-safe modeling dataset called cleaned_model_nfl.

The next steps are to split the data, define the baseline and logistic models, fit them using resampling, and present their performance in a comparison table. After that, I plan to expand the modeling pipeline with additional model types and richer feature engineering.
